cases.title: EEG alpha power with eyes open and eyes closed
cases.context: Researchers interested in the alpha rhythm of the electroencephalogram (EEG) (an 8 to 12 Hz oscillation recorded from the scalp) did a study to evaluate whether alpha power over the occipital cortex (the visual area at the back of the brain) depends on whether the eyes are open. Each subject was evaluated during 3 minutes of rest with the eyes open (measurement 1) and again during 3 minutes of rest with the eyes closed (measurement 2). Alpha power was recorded at electrode Oz (a scalp site at the back of the head) in microvolts squared (μV²).
tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that alpha power is different in these two states? Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. DO NOT use R.

hypotheses.nullWords: Closing the eyes produces no change in mean occipital alpha power (the true mean eyes closed minus eyes open difference is zero).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Closing the eyes changes mean occipital alpha power (the true mean eyes closed minus eyes open difference is not zero).

cases.symbols: \(d_i\) (difference in subject \(i\)), \(\bar d\) (mean difference), \(s_d\) (SD of the differences), \(s_{\bar d}\) (standard error of the mean difference), \(\delta\) (true mean difference), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Each subject is measured under both conditions, so the procedure is the paired t test on the within-subject differences. Closing the eyes produces no change in mean occipital alpha power (the true mean eyes closed minus eyes open difference is zero). Closing the eyes changes mean occipital alpha power (the true mean eyes closed minus eyes open difference is not zero).

steps.title: Form one difference per subject
steps.words: Subtract in the same direction for every subject (eyes closed minus eyes open). Subject 3 has a difference of the opposite sign, and it stays in the list with its sign. The analysis now uses only these 10 numbers.

steps.title: Calculate the mean difference
steps.words: The mean difference estimates the true mean change \(\delta\) in μV².

steps.title: Calculate the SD of the differences
steps.words: Square each deviation of a difference from the mean difference, add them, divide by \(n-1\), and take the root.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the mean difference
steps.words: The standard error describes how much the mean difference varies from sample to sample.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
general: t=\frac{\bar d-\delta}{s_{\bar d}}=\frac{\bar d}{s_{\bar d}}\quad(\delta=0\text{ under }H_0)
steps.words: Under the null hypothesis the true mean difference is zero, so the numerator is the mean difference itself.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Start with α = 0.05. Use row 9 and the two-tailed 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.262.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic exceeds the 0.05 cutoff, so reject the null hypothesis. In row 9 it also passes every stricter column up to the 0.001 column (4.781), so P < 0.001.

cases.conclusion: The mean eyes closed minus eyes open difference is 4.84 μV², t = 6.75941 with 9 degrees of freedom, above 2.262. Reject the null hypothesis. There is a difference in occipital alpha power between the two states, and alpha power is higher with the eyes closed (P < 0.001).

tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the pressure pain threshold is different in these two states? Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. DO NOT use R.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: The TENS session produces no change in the mean pressure pain threshold (the true mean after minus before difference is zero).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The TENS session changes the mean pressure pain threshold (the true mean after minus before difference is not zero).

cases.title: Amygdala BOLD response to neutral and fearful faces, analyzed as two groups
cases.context: In a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study, ten subjects viewed neutral faces and fearful faces in the scanner. The blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal change in the amygdala (an almond-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe), expressed as the percent change from a fixation baseline, was recorded for each subject in both conditions. An analyst then compared the two columns as if they came from two separate groups of ten different people. Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed.
tasks: (i) Treat the two columns as two separate groups of ten different people. Based on that analysis, is there evidence that the amygdala BOLD signal change is different for neutral and fearful faces? DO NOT use R.

(ii) A paired analysis of the same data gives t = 5.31412 with 9 degrees of freedom. Using only your calculations for Part (i) and this value, state which analysis fits the design of this study. Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: The mean amygdala BOLD signal change is the same for neutral faces and fearful faces.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The mean amygdala BOLD signal change is different for neutral faces and fearful faces.

cases.symbols: \(\bar x_i\) (group sample mean), \(s_i\) (group sample SD), \(n_i\) (group size), \(s^2\) (pooled variance), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: The unpaired t test compares two group means as if every number came from a different person. The mean amygdala BOLD signal change is the same for neutral faces and fearful faces.

steps.title: Calculate the group means and SDs
steps.words: The SDs are large compared with the gap between the two means because the subjects differ a lot from one another in how strongly the amygdala responds to any face.

steps.title: Pool the variances
steps.words: Each group variance is weighted by its own degrees of freedom.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error and t
steps.words: The numerator is the same 0.079 percentage points of signal change as the paired analysis, but the denominator now carries the between-subject spread.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Start with α = 0.05. Use row 18 and the two-tailed 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.101.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: The unpaired test does not reject the null hypothesis (P > 0.05). The paired test on the same numbers gives t = 5.31412 with 9 degrees of freedom and rejects it (P < 0.001), because pairing removes the large differences between subjects and leaves only each subject's own change. The same subjects appear in both columns, so the paired test is the analysis that fits this design.

cases.conclusion: Analyzed as two separate groups, t = 0.781549 with 18 degrees of freedom is below 2.101, so the unpaired test finds no evidence of a difference (P > 0.05). The paired test on the same data gives t = 5.31412 with 9 degrees of freedom and finds a difference (P < 0.001). The same ten subjects were scanned in both conditions, so the paired test fits the design, and ignoring the pairing hides the difference between the two conditions.

cases.title: V1 BOLD response at three checkerboard contrasts

tasks: Is there a difference in the V1 BOLD signal change among the three contrast levels? Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. DO NOT use R. (Note: If a difference exists, do not identify which groups are different.)

steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Start with α = 0.05. Use numerator column \(\nu_n=2\) and denominator row \(\nu_d=10\). The lightface (P < .05) value is 4.10. The boldface (P < .01) value is 7.56.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: F exceeds the lightface 0.05 value, so reject the null hypothesis. It does not reach the boldface 0.01 value, so 0.01 < P < 0.05.

cases.conclusion: F = 5.61816 with 2 and 10 degrees of freedom exceeds 4.10 but not the boldface 7.56. Reject the null hypothesis at α = 0.05. There is a difference in the mean heat pain threshold among the three conditions (P < 0.05).

cases.title: Vigilance reaction time at three times of day
cases.context: In a study looking at alertness across the day, five subjects each completed a psychomotor vigilance task (pressing a button as soon as a counter appears on a screen) at 8 AM, 2 PM and 8 PM on the same day. Mean reaction time was recorded in milliseconds (ms).
tasks: Is there a difference in reaction time over time? Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. DO NOT use R.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{at least one treatment mean differs}
hypotheses.nullWords: Mean reaction time is the same at 8 AM, 2 PM and 8 PM.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: At least one time of day has a different mean reaction time.

cases.symbols: \(x_{ts}\) (response to treatment \(t\) in subject \(s\)), \(\bar S_s\) (subject mean), \(\bar T_t\) (treatment mean), \(\bar X\) (grand mean), \(m\) (number of treatments), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(SS\) (sum of squares), \(MS\) (mean square), \(F\) (F statistic).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_A:\text{not all treatment means are equal}
steps.words: Every subject receives every treatment, so the procedure is repeated measures ANOVA. Mean reaction time is the same at 8 AM, 2 PM and 8 PM. At least one time of day has a different mean reaction time.

steps.title: Calculate the subject means
steps.words: Average across the 3 treatments within each subject.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment means and the grand mean
steps.words: Average down each treatment column across the 5 subjects, then average all 15 observations.

steps.title: Calculate the sum of squares within subjects
steps.words: Each subject's own spread around their own mean is added up. Differences between subjects (SS between subjects = 10223.1) are set aside.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment sum of squares
steps.words: The factor n appears because each treatment mean is based on n subjects.

steps.title: Calculate the residual sum of squares
steps.words: What remains of the within-subject variation after the treatment effect is removed is the residual.

steps.title: Calculate the mean squares and F
steps.words: A large F means the treatment means differ more than the leftover within-subject noise would explain.

steps.title: Find the critical F
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Start with α = 0.05. Use numerator column \(\nu_n=2\) and denominator row \(\nu_d=8\). The lightface (P < .05) value is 4.46. The boldface (P < .01) value is 8.65.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: F is below the lightface 0.05 value, so the null hypothesis is not rejected. The table has no column above 0.05, so the P range is P > 0.05. The subjects differ a lot from one another, but that spread is set aside and does not enter F.

cases.conclusion: F = 1.72965 with 2 and 8 degrees of freedom is below 4.46. Do not reject the null hypothesis. These data give no evidence that reaction time on the vigilance task is different at the three times of day (P > 0.05).

questions.stem: In the EEG alpha power study (ten subjects, eyes closed minus eyes open), what is the mean difference \(\bar d\)?
questions.why: The ten differences sum to 48.4 μV², with the negative difference of subject 3 kept as negative. Dividing by n = 10 gives 4.84 μV².

questions.stem: In the TENS pressure pain threshold study (eleven subjects, after minus before), what is the SD of the differences \(s_d\)?
questions.why: The squared deviations sum to 2054.55. Dividing by n − 1 = 10 gives 205.455, and its root is 14.3337 kPa. Dividing by n, stopping at the variance, or dividing again by the root of n gives the other values.

questions.stem: In the P300 sleep loss study (ten subjects, sleep deprived minus rested), what is the t statistic for the test that fits the design?
questions.why: Each subject is measured in both states, so t is the mean difference over its standard error, -1.24/0.532958 = -2.32664. The value -1.18835 is what the unpaired test gives on the same numbers.

questions.stem: In the amygdala BOLD study, the two columns are treated as two separate groups of ten. What is the unpaired (pooled) t statistic?
questions.why: The pooled variance is 0.0510872, so the standard error is 0.101081 and t = 0.079/0.101081 = 0.781549. The value 5.31412 is the paired t on the same data.

questions.stem: In the cold pressor study, R prints a 95 percent confidence interval for the mean music minus silence difference. What is the lower endpoint when it is calculated by hand with the printed cutoff \(t_{0.05}(9)=2.262\)?
questions.why: The interval is the mean difference plus or minus the printed cutoff times the standard error, 8 − 2.262(2.87518) = 1.49634 s. It matches the lower endpoint in the R output to about two decimals, and it is above 0.

questions.stem: In the heat pain threshold study (six subjects, three cream conditions), what is the F statistic?
questions.why: F is the treatment mean square over the residual mean square, 1.76722/0.314556 = 5.61816. Leaving the between-subject spread in the denominator, as an ANOVA for separate groups does, gives a much smaller value.

questions.stem: Twelve listeners have their speech reception threshold in noise (lowest signal-to-noise ratio at which half of the sentences are repeated correctly) measured without a hearing aid and again with a hearing aid. Which procedure fits this design?
options: An unpaired t test on the two columns, with \(\nu=22\)
A paired t test on the twelve within-subject differences, with \(\nu=11\)
A chi-square test on a 2 by 2 table of the thresholds
An unpaired t test on the twelve differences against the twelve aided thresholds
questions.why: Each listener is measured in both states on an interval scale, so the test is the paired t test on the differences. The degrees of freedom are n − 1 = 11.

questions.stem: Ten patients rate migraine pain before and after a nerve block. The paired t test rejects the null hypothesis, but an unpaired t test on the same two columns does not. What explains the unpaired result?
options: The unpaired test uses fewer degrees of freedom, so its cutoff is larger
The unpaired test changes the mean difference in the numerator
The unpaired test is one-sided, so it needs a larger t
The unpaired standard error keeps the large differences between patients, so the same mean change is divided by a much larger number
questions.why: Both tests have the same numerator. The unpaired denominator is built from the spread between patients, while the paired denominator uses only the spread of each patient's own change.

questions.stem: Eight drummers each tap along with a metronome at three tempos, and timing error is recorded at each tempo. In the repeated measures ANOVA, which degrees of freedom are used to find the critical F?
questions.why: The numerator uses m − 1 = 2 and the denominator uses the residual, (n − 1)(m − 1) = 7 × 2 = 14. The value 21 belongs to an ANOVA with three separate groups of eight, and 16 is the full within-subject degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: R output for a paired t test of resting tremor amplitude in ten patients before and after a drug includes "p-value = 0.1142" and the lines "95 percent confidence interval:" and "-0.82 6.41". Which reading of the output is correct?
options: The interval contains 0 and the p-value is above 0.05, so the null hypothesis is not rejected
The interval is mostly positive, so there is a difference at the 0.05 level
The p-value is the probability that the drug has no effect
The interval shows that 95 percent of the subjects changed by between −0.82 and 6.41
questions.why: A 95 percent interval for the mean difference that contains 0 goes with a two-sided P above 0.05. Both lines of the output give the same decision, which is not to reject the null hypothesis.

notes: All data are invented for practice. Critical values are the printed ones in sources/tables/t_table.pdf (rows 9, 10, 18) and F_table.pdf page 1 (columns 2, rows 6, 8, 10). No df row had to be bracketed.
Differences are always measurement 2 minus measurement 1, as in the ref pairedR case. n20-p300-sleep-loss has a negative t (answer is the signed t, the table comparison uses |t|).

Outcome mix. Do not reject: n20-tens-pressure-pain, n20-amygdala-faces-unpaired (by design), n20-vigilance-time-of-day-rmanova. Close to a cutoff: n20-p300-sleep-loss (|t| just above t0.05(9) = 2.262). Between 0.05 and 0.01: n20-heat-pain-cream-rmanova.

n20-amygdala-faces-unpaired shows the raw Subject table (the ref unpaired case shows a summary table) so that the means, SDs and the quoted paired t can be recomputed from raw data. Its values keys match the ref case.

The two s20pairedR cases store real Rscript output (R 4.6.1) in values.rOutput and values.rCode, like the ref case. The step words quote the output without colons because of the no colon rule, so the exact printed lines are the ones in values.rOutput.
Unlike the ref cases, conclusions and step words contain no colons or semicolons (spec rule), so 'Reject the null hypothesis.' is followed by a new sentence.

Style review. His own phrases are restored in context and tasks with their punctuation, for example "(Note: If a difference exists, do not identify which groups are different.)" and his R ask for the paired R cases, so tasks may contain colons and the check script allows colons and semicolons in context and tasks only. The test name was removed from the three repeated measures titles.
